@bayesianboy There is so much successful work done by ML in science. There’s a least a decade of work in both astrophysics and particle physics. As philosophers of science we must be clearer and open-minded as to where and when novel technologies offer genuine advances. Is part of our job.

@bayesianboy And yet, I still think there is a sense that in SOME instances (including hallucinations) it is the artifact that is erring. For those of us in phil of computation and science, there was a similar discussion about malfunction/disfunction in science software 10 years ago.

I know there are serious reservations abt the corporate structures behind peer review. But that is a diff issue. In any case, putting together a template to facilitate peer reviews and get rid of anxiety and procrastination. Mainly for myself, but let me know if you’d like a copy

90% of peer reviews in phil could be done by reading the paper and working ~30 minutes on a response. And reading recent papers in your AOS is already something you should be doing anyway. Someone’s sending you the latest to your inbox and asking your opinion! How cool is that?

Part of what we don’t hear in graduate school is how integral peer review is to our discipline and to our job. Some see it as this extra external (unpaid) burden and not an opportunity to assess/engage with/learn from the state of the art.

Some people don’t realize that editors mainly only send out things that they already deemed interesting/worthy of review. What they need is a hyper-specialized set of eyes to fill in the blanks of why this is or isn’t worthy of publication.

Although ideally there would be a thorough, thoughtful and meaningful engagement with a peer’s work, practically speaking editors need only 3 things: a) summary of arguments, b) section on minor issues (readability, structure), c) section on major issues (conceptual, lit, etc.)

Hence, a lot of anxiety, procrastination, hit/miss, motley approaches, cynical engagement, missed opportunities. Some EICs tried to fix it through an incentivizing strategy: promise of possible publication. More anxiety and procrastination ensued. I know from personal experience.

No one systematically teaches you how to approach/write reviews. There’s only 2 sources of knowledge:

1- advisor/other tells you ~what to do
 
(iff you get a reason to ask- e.g. you are asked to review, you are curious)

2- You see other reviews

(Iff you are publishing)

Importantly, Bacon’s is a recipe for a social epistemology (conducted but not determined socially). This implies that several things must be in place: institutions, standards, etc. His project was a radical reform of education, only fully realized by the 19th/20th centuries.

For Bacon, steps to true induction after getting privileged instances from the tables are:

-support + refinement of induction
-adapt inquiry to target
-prioritize sub targets
-parametrize/define inquiry
-elucidate practical consequences
-prepare investigation
-create axioms

3/4

For Bacon, this 1st step towards proper induction requires looking at:

+ instances
- instances
correlated instances of X and degrees/deviations thereof 

From these one derives through exclusion plausible/privileged instances which then undergo a 9 step process of inquiry. 2/4

Week 7 of Bacon’s epistemology. We learn his 3 tables derive several hypothesis that were novel for the time.

- heat IS motion
- color IS light refraction
- taste IS smell
- the extended mind

Importantly, the tables are just the first step of 10 towards ‘proper’ induction.🧵

In any case, things I’ve been thinking about: a) going beyond utilitarian harm mitigation in ethics, b) how far humans have got in automated tech, c) how conservative AI ethics discourse really is.

Also, notice that the AI ethics is almost completely taken over by utilitarian and conservative assumptions about harms and mitigation and not ethical questions. There are deeper axiological questions that we need to ask about our relationship to AI and its automation powers.

In ethics of AI, we shouldn’t conflate AI uses/applications with AI, nor the intentions of makers/designers/investors with the tech. Or the political landscape in which a tech is developed with the tech. 

https://t.co/B2ezs0PeIX

While relevant, they are not the same thing.

Note that I’m not talking about the interface you engage with, or the images or output generated, or how outputs are spread on social media or the bots transformers/ML/DNNs are used for. These are applications of AI, not AI. I’m talking about the technical artifacts themselves.

GPTs/LLMs are awesome as part of a continuum of epistemic technologies. But, they also have deep and novel ethical implications. E.g. we don’t have an ethics for epistemic technologies; we govern with but don’t regulate foundational tech: the clock, the calendar, gears, etc. Also

Compared to other machines made to be epistemic technologies, LLMs are an awesome technical accomplishment. Think of the process architecture, the statistical methods, the scale, the compute power, and compare it to pulley theory, Babbage’s engine, tide predictors, or computers. https://t.co/SrFuIonrNk

AI/LLMs seem to meet all the conditions for being an epistemic tech: mainly designed, developed and/or deployed

- in epistemic contexts (inquiry)
- to carry out epistemic operations (i.e. recognition, prediction, inference) 
- on epistemic content (tokens, data, symbols)

an epistemic technology doesn’t necessarily need to be knowledge-conducive or even knowledge-apt to be epistemic. Like other artifacts, they can fail at their job and still be identified by what they’re supposed to do (like a bad 🪛). So, however bad they may be, LLMs qualify. 2/

When it comes to AI/other computational methods in science, we have to decide which imaginary (@SabinaLeonelli) we want to live with: a world in which we do what was ACTUALLY done with the telescope or one in which we accept instruments like oracle believers accept magic rocks.

Neglecting the history of science and the philosophy of technology risks appealing to simple epistemic entitlements to justify our reliance on new technology. This is simply inadequate for novel technologies in scientific practice. 
https://t.co/13JfxcSXN8

In fact, a whole institution was developed to help with such efforts and to establish best practices related to telescope development:

https://t.co/yegwcSdTqZ

So rather than calling for a moratorium, resources were concentrated in reliability assessments.

New texts had to be devised (popular poems could be guessed); new fonts were necessary (some letters could be guessed); new paper had to be invented (shadows in the print could give the text away). It was a multidisciplinary effort: astronomers, mathematicians, lens makers, etc.

For the telescope to be sanctioned as a reliable scientific instrument it took a couple of decades and incredible efforts, even the establishment of a whole industry of standards, practices and materials. Not only did they test telescopes, even the tests had to be tested.

Kepler had to run multiple evening sightings with a borrowed Galilean telescope with very specific controls in place: "trustworthy" witnesses would each draw what they saw in the dark and then compare findings. And even this was not enough for the larger community of scientist.

The only reason why Galileo and Kepler accepted it was because they understood much of the theoretical aspects of both astronomy and optics, i.e., it wasn't fully opaque to them. Galileo was famously proud of the fact that he constructed his telescope from pure theory.

What they neglect is that the telescope was not accepted as a SCIENTIFIC instrument for a long time after its development. Galileo was literally laughed out of Bologna when he tried to showcase his version of it and people wrote to Kepler about how his instrument "deceived."

How can we fairly flip the classroom in this manner? In the face of generative AI, how can we create a space where presence and active engagement become the foundation of learning, while still leveraging the benefits of written text? Suggestions greatly appreciated.

When I resume teaching next year, I am thinking on focusing on fostering meaningful conversation. Embracing the in-person classroom experience will be key. Hence, attendance **and** PARTICIPATION will hold equal or greater importance than written assignments.

Hence, for philosophers, the pressure from chatGPT-like tech is distinct. We can differentiate our work in the classroom and among peers from writing. Yet, like all academics, we must adapt while responding to institutional conventions. How do we do this?

In philosophy, the answer isn't obvious: great thinkers have existed despite their subpar writing & many good writers are not great thinkers. Furthermore, Plato himself wondered if writing hindered thought. Conversation, it was argued, is where thinking takes shape, unrestricted.

However, the hardest questions emerge when we consider how to actually impart such education in the classroom. Here’s the rub: Isn't thinking+inquiry grounded in articulation, and isn't articulation best developed in writing? If so, isn’t tech like chat-GPT a threat to inquiry?

Philosophers have some rough and ready answers to these questions. Roughly speaking, to us, education is meant to enrich inquiry. Our focus: mastering inquiry and valuing reasons over conclusions. Questions are key. Written answers matter, but they're just part of what we value.

At the discipline level, questions like "what are we teaching in our discipline?" emerge (think of English composition courses). Moving to the education as a whole level, bigger questions arise: "what is education?", "what are we educating for?", and "what are we educating in?"
These conversations raise questions at different levels about #GPT4 , #ChatGPT  and  #LLMs in general: challenges to specific disciplines, education as a whole, and the practical classroom space.

So, benchmark datasets in ML #AI:

- are developed in isolation from parts of the world
- 'Plopped' into parts of the world
- unilaterally affect the social fabric there

Hence, sociotechnical frameworks are either wrong or inadequate to understand AI in the developing world.

Most OA datasets are being designed in the developed world, even if the labor is offshored. They are also becoming more and more concentrated bc of how difficult they are to construct. Furthermore, because of technological lock-in (@SabinaLeonelli, 2016) change is unlikely.

Mainly, when we consider the way open access benchmark datasets + pretrained models are used in the Developing World. A sociotechnical understanding of tech can only elucidate some aspects of tech development where the tech is produced, not where it is economically imposed.

I presented at Stanford, arguing that the sociotechnical framework— which postulates that technologies are not developed in isolation, that tech isn't just "plopped" into society, and that it can't unidirectionally affect social change— is out of touch when it comes to AI + ML https://t.co/jAjGV0DqIa

TLDR: I assign 1 term paper. Done one week at a time over ten weeks. I provide templates for sections of paper but they choose what they write about. It’s formulaic but it makes them think a lot about their ideas/beliefs + why/how to defend them. It’s impervious to plagiarism/AI.

That is it. General thoughts: “good” writers/some phil students hate it (something about style/voice); “struggling writers”/CS/STEM/ESL students LOVE it (programmed structure/no rush/no anxiety); Final paper looks like a longer version of picture. https://t.co/T4xMWTkAQ0

W10: Edit to your liking w/o altering the structure; take a minute to compare/contrast original blurb to new introduction section (tell me what changed about your ideas + what you learned about your ideas from the changes at the end of your paper); take a deep breath; submit.

W9: Add descriptive/straightforward title; cut motivation paragraph + use it as introduction to your paper; write a brief conclusion (you can use template provided for either); identify sections of your paper the following way: Introduction, analysis, objection, conclusion.

W8: Consult comments made to your entry on  W6; following template, thoughtfully replace variables/choice of argumentative strategy to charitably consider an objection to your view. Following second paragraph in template, replace variables/choice of strategy to respond. https://t.co/ULTWgLLXQg

W7: Following template provided, replace variables (from week 5) and write a paragraph that explains, expands and exemplifies each premise in your arguments in the order provided in the thesis statement. https://t.co/jtgvUEcoMI

W6: Turn all personal references or motives in your motivation paragraph ( W4) into statements of fact about general importance of your topic; POST your thesis statement and new motivation paragraph on graded discussion forum for others to see; reply to 2 entries constructively.

W5: Following the template in picture, replace the variables in the following way:
X, Y, Z= conclusions of each arguments
a, b, etc.= premises supporting X, Y or Z resp.
i, ii, n= the reasons you cited that make your premises true: evidence, definitions, sources, authority, etc. https://t.co/UcZQMKYLwD

W4: Choose 1-3 arguments you really need/want to work with; for EACH PREMISE of each argument write down two reasons/sources of evidence that make that premise true or likely true. Also, write a brief motivation paragraph for topic of choice.

W3: Visit https://t.co/xTtr9gwXa6; test your arguments vs. fallacies; ID which argument fits what fallacy and fix it e.g., remove appeals to emotion, distractions, etc. Rewrite your arguments and resubmit them as in prompt 2. No fallacy found= explain strength of each argument.

W2: Return to prompt 1 and extract all the statements; turn any questions into statements; add statements if needed; ID main statements you want to defend and the secondary statements you think support them. Formalize in premise/conclusion form. ID number of arguments.

Week 1: Write a short free-form paragraph/blurb (5-10 sentences max. <300 words) about something that you think is important and/or interesting, something that you feel strongly about or that you want to learn more about related to the topic of this class.

The assignment is a single paper written in the span of 10 weeks. Each week they submit part of it and they build upon the previous week until a full paper is done by week 9. Basic concepts (e.g. arguments, premises, etc.) are explained in class. Here are the basic prompts:

Caveats: this is a condensed version of actual prompts; prompts include templates and examples; designed to help struggling writers overcome anxiety of writing; yes, it is formulaic but designed to make students think first and foremost. Students have NO access to future prompts.
